correctness.rationale: For g=x²−1 over F2, Frobenius gives g^N(x)≡x^(2^N) for even N, x^(2^N)+1 for odd N. Thus F=(g^N)^2+c≡x^(2^(N+1)) for even N and x^(2^(N+1))+1 for odd N. Even N constant F(0)=c≡2 mod4; odd N shifted constant F(1)=c≡2 mod4. Hence the unshifted/shifted monic polynomial is 2-Eisenstein for every N>=0. With f=x²+c and g=x²−1, published Theorem 1.8 has rad(2)|2 and g^i(0)=0,-1 alternately; its squarefree list for N>=1 is exactly {c,c+1}. Its second prime test 4∤((-c)²+c)=c(c+1) automatically holds. Independent full exact integer polynomial expansion for c=2,6,10,14,22 and N=0..4 checked all parity coefficients and constant valuations. Tests support but do not prove the infinite statement; the symbolic induction and cited conditional theorem do.
residual_risks: Dependence of monogeneity equivalence on published Theorem 1.8; irreducibility itself proved directly

originality.rationale: DECISIVE STRONGER PRIOR COVERAGE: this is a single-polynomial iterate in disguise. With f(x)=1−x² and g(x)=x²−1, for every m>=1 one has f^m(x)=−g^m(x). Therefore F_(c,N)(x)=−(f^(N+1)(x)−(c+1)). König–Smith–Wolske arXiv:2412.10358v3, Theorem 4.2, already characterizes all dynamically monogenic iterates of f=1−x^d. Substituting d=2 and a=c+1 gives c,c+1 squarefree and (−c) not congruent to 1 mod4; the latter is automatic for c≡2 mod4. Thus the principal infinite monogeneity classification is an immediate special case of the published 2025 theorem, which also supplies dynamical irreducibility when those conditions hold. The extra irreducibility for nonsquarefree parameters comes from an elementary parity Eisenstein check but does not rescue the overall final classification from substantive prior coverage.
residual_risks: The elementary alternating 2-Eisenstein observation for nonsquarefree c is not literally asserted by Theorem 4.2; it is correct but cannot rescue originality of the full already-covered monogeneity classification.
This rejection is a scientific prior-implication judgment, not a literature access failure.
